prompt: At 10:00 a popular catalog key expires on every application instance. Cache hit ratio falls, origin database traffic rises forty times, latency grows, retries begin, and the cache remains reachable. Diagnose and recover without flushing the entire cache or permanently serving stale prices.
directAnswer: Bind the user operation, cache layer and key, cache-key version, TTL/expiry distribution, request rate, hit/miss/eviction counters, per-key origin queries, origin pool/queue/latency, retries and returned revision. This pattern is a synchronized expiry and cache stampede, not proof that the cache server is down. Contain retry amplification and protect the origin with admission or shedding. Allow one bounded owner per key to refresh while peers wait, use stale-while-revalidate only within the business-approved freshness window, and keep a hard stale limit for price correctness. Add randomized TTL jitter or proactive refresh based on measured demand so keys do not expire together. A distributed lock alone is insufficient unless its timeout, fencing and failure behavior are correct; request coalescing with an authoritative version is usually easier. Verify origin queries per logical miss, cache fill latency, hit recovery, freshness/revision, user success and tail latency, then confirm the key can expire again without a herd. Do not flush all keys: that destroys evidence and creates a larger cold-start miss storm.
foundation: A cache miss transfers work to the origin. Many simultaneous misses for one key can multiply one needed refresh into thousands of origin requests; availability depends on coalescing, bounded stale policy, jitter, admission and origin capacity.
reasoningSteps: Bind user operation cache layer key and revision.
Correlate synchronized expiry with miss and origin amplification.
Separate eviction expiry invalidation and connectivity.
Bound retries and protect origin capacity.
Coalesce refresh by key with safe timeout/failure behavior.
Apply only business-approved bounded stale serving.
Introduce TTL jitter or proactive refresh.
Verify freshness correctness and one-refresh behavior.
Test the next expiry and cold-start envelope.
Record capacity ownership and runbook changes.
seniorAnswer: I measure origin amplification per logical key and protect the origin first. I use one bounded refresh owner, revision-aware fill, TTL jitter and an explicit stale window. I do not optimize hit ratio at the cost of returning an unsafe price, and I test expiry under representative concurrency.
weakAnswer: Redis is slow; increase memory, set a one-day TTL, flush it, and add three retries.
whyWeak: Reachability and memory do not explain synchronized expiry; flushing and retries amplify misses, while a long arbitrary TTL creates unbounded business staleness.

followUps.prompt: Why not use one global lock?
followUps.answer: It serializes unrelated keys and creates a shared failure point. Coalesce at the key/invariant scope with bounded wait and failure behavior.
Only when the operation can safely tolerate the bounded age, the response exposes or records staleness as required, and security/correctness decisions do not fail open.

followUps.prompt: What if the hot key itself exceeds one partition's capacity?
followUps.answer: Cache or replicate read-only copies, coalesce work, precompute, shed excess, or change the invariant with controlled allocation; arbitrary key salting breaks single-key writes unless aggregation and correctness are redesigned.
